                                    THOMAS F. GREEN’S REPLY
              TO APPLICANTS’ EXCEPTION TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION


           ON BEHALF OF INTERVENORS THOMAS F. GREEN AND HEIDI A. GREEN
                            LIVING TRUST AND DOS BROTHERS LLC

                        Thomas F. Green, P.E., on behalf of and in his role as

                 Trustee of The Thomas F. Green and Heidi A. Green Living Trust

                                 and on behalf of Dos Brothers LLC

  Respectfully files this pro se’ Reply to Applicants’ Exception to the SOAH Proposal for Decision

         and stipulates that all parties may treat his testimony as though filed under oath.




                                              Preface

Thomas F. Green (Green), currently a pro se’ intervenor, presents this filing in good faith and with
factually sound backing. Green is not an attorney and is inexperienced in preparing and filing this
Reply: it is his first rodeo as they say. Accordingly, deference and forbearance regarding the form of
the Reply is humbly invited and will be welcomed and much appreciated. It is presumed the SOAH
will view the facts to be of higher importance than an attorney-like presentation of them. Green’s
reply, that of a “lay person” (as the Applicants call the intervenor witnesses), has immense merit
based on the evidentiary record, a record created by one of the Applicants (Oncor).

Green’s Reply will endeavor to use the “plain language” professed to be used many times by the
Applicants in their filed Exceptions.

It should be noted that Green has, out of time necessity, constrained his Reply to one common
thread argument in the Applicants’ Exceptions. Green would have materially more replies to other
of the Applicants’ assertions had time been sufficient to develop the replies.

In addition to the specifics cited in this Reply, Green has relied in a few instances upon his Direct
Testimony in Docket 59475 (Item 4546 and Supplements 4689, 4726, and 4792), testimony which
has generally been un-challenged, un-rebutted, un-contested, and un-cross-examined. It
therefore also serves as evidentiary record.



                                                 [2]
 A. Green’s Foundational Premise.

 The Applicants’ argument regarding the interdependence of Import Path 2 and other Import
 Paths is factually flawed, as directly and decidedly supported by the evidentiary record. The
 assertion that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) or other Dockets or Import Paths are
 sufficient to justify Import Path 2, because the PBRP is claimed to be an integrated Plan, is
 materially deficient.

B. Applicants’ Assertions.

 The Applicants, in various and repeated ways, assert that the Import Path 2 cannot be separated
 from the other Import Paths because they are all part of a single integrated Plan. With various
 words in various places, they assert all the Import Paths are integrated and interdependent.
 Green did not, at one point in time, disagree with the assertion. Green, too, thought it a powerful
 and logical argument. The SOAH agreed. Green and SOAH were overruled by the PUC upon
 an appeal filing to the PUC by one of the Applicants (Oncor).

 Upon that PUC ruling, the ship christened “Integrated and Interdependent” sailed, not to return
 to port in the three Import Paths of the PBRP (or the Plan). The three Import Paths became
 “independent.”

 The Applicants’ erred assertion, a common thread throughout its Exceptions, is that all the
 Import Paths are integrated and interdependent.

 Below, in numbered and italicized paragraphs, are presented a few excerpted common thread
 examples in the Applicants’ Exception to the Proposal for Decision (Docket 59475, Item
 6484).

 Specifically:

           1. “The Import Path 2 Projects are not an untested solution to a hypothetical
              problem that is unlikely to materialize. They are, rather, an indispensable
              component of a legislatively directed, Commission-approved, ERCOT -planned
              transmission solution for the Permian Basin region.” (page 8).

   The bases of Import Path 2 are absolutely untested and well-recognized to be highly
   speculative. The Import Path 2 bases are exceedingly low confidence and subject to much
   continuing change and volatility. The assertion that Import Path 2 is indispensable
   (interdependent) with respect to Import Paths 1 and 3, in plain language, is woefully
   incorrect as is demonstrated herein. Even the Applicants’ own words in No. 6 below testify
   that Import Path 2 is “recommended.” Recommended and indispensable are not the same in
   any universe.

           2. “First, the Commission and six presiding officers across three other dockets have
              already found that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”) alone is
              sufficient to establish the need for the recommended 765 kV transmission
              infrastructure.5 The Commission granted CCNs for both projects comprising
              Import Path 1, finding in each case that the PBRP establishes the need for
              additional service in the Permian Basin. That finding applies with equal force
                                            [3]
               to the Import Path 2 Project.” (page 8).

The Applicants’ assertion is an extrapolation of tremendous proportions. Need for Import
Paths 1 or 3 cannot be used as justification for Need in Import Path 2. There is no equal
force. Import Path 2 Need and CCN 59475 must be proven, not merely associated as part of
a common Plan. Evidence and conclusion from one case do not extend by some magic
evidentiary transmission to another case. One Docket cannot decide another. One Import
Path cannot decide another.

         3.    “The Commission’s findings regarding Import Path 1, the ALJs’
              recommendation regarding Import Path 3, and the underlying evidentiary basis
              for both Import Paths 1 and 3, are equally true for the Import Path 2 Projects.”
              (page 15)

The assertion is Import Path 2 need must equal Import Path 1 and 3 since the granting of
Import Paths 1 and 3 were proposed by the SOAH. Green finds no conceivable logic or
reasoning for such an assertion. What would the reasoning be if Import Path 1 or 3 were
proposed by the SOAH to be denied? Would all therefore be denied? Why even have
separate Dockets? Why even have a CCN process? Are all Dockets automatically approved
if but one is proven to be needed? The evidence in each Docket, each Import Path, must
support itself from foundation to conclusion with credible substantial evidence. Evidence
does not support any imminent need for Import Path 2.

         4 . “The Import Path 2 Projects are an integrated component of the PBRP and a core
             component of ERCOT’s statewide transmission reliability plan.11 All three PBRP
             import paths are critical to the overall PBRP because, as ERCOT explained in
             the PBRP study report, without them the Permian Basin load growth cannot be
             fully served.” ( p a g e 1 5 ) .

T h e e x p l i c i t a s s e r t i o n i s t h a t Im p o r t P a t h 2 i s a n i n t e g r a t e d c o m p o n e n t
of not only the PBRP, but also the statewide Strategic Transmission
Expansion Plan, a Plan not identified in legislation, but instead created
by ERCOT and its TSPs and other “stakeholders.” As is clearly and
decisively demonstrated, Import Path 2 is not an inseparable or
integrated critical service Path in the near term. As admitted by the
Applicants’ excerpt No. 6 below, ERCOT merely “recommends” Import
Path 2. Furthermore, the Permian Basin growth has been, is currently,
a n d w i l l b e s e r v e d s a n s t h e Im p o r t P a t h 2 t r a n s m i s s i o n l i n e s .

         5. “Applicants except to the PFD’s need analysis because it affords greater weight
            to the opinion testimony of lay witnesses, none of whom have or even purport to
            claim any expertise in transmission planning or electrical engineering, Nor is
            anyone in the PBRP than it does to the consistent, well-documented
            recommendations of ERCOT, the entity the Texas Legislature and the
            Commission have entrusted with planning the transmission system to ensure
            system reliability.” (page 16).

The language’s implicit assertion is that credibility cannot be extended to lay witnesses, who

                                                     [4]
 the Applicants must believe possess only moronic intelligence. Instead, the Applicants seem
to allege only the PUC and the SOAH and the ERCOT and the Applicants possess all of the
relevant knowledge. Brash, to say the least.

The Applicants’ assertion is that the intervenors who have spent literally tens of thousands
of hours applying what they already knew and deeply researching great volumes of data and
information, even those who are experienced professional engineers in related physics and
electrical engineering (e.g., Green), possess none of the apparently covert knowledge
needed to have credible input. Green opines that the Applicants’ assertions of intervenor lay
witnesses being un-credible… is itself un-credible: the Applicants had multiple
opportunities (three times with Green) to cross examine lay witnesses, yet did not do so.
Perhaps Applicants thought it better to not risk bringing credible information to the ALJs
forefront in a Hearing on the Merits.

If Intervenors cannot be qualified witnesses, why conduct the process at all, as it would be
a purely performative charade.

The Applicants’ assertion is that whoever it might have been that created the PBRP is to be
afforded total and unscrutinized credibility despite the facts that: the authors are not
disclosed; the document itself is not an engineered Plan; the authors, if they were known,
cannot be questioned as they are not parties to the proceedings; there is no independent
scrutiny in evidence; and there is no professional accountability to the PBRP. None. Zero.
Zilch.

The little that is known about the PBRP authorship and stakeholders is that TSPs, the ones
who benefit from the PBRP, were included in the stakeholder club. Independent public
advocates or landowners, the only ones adversely affected by the PBRP, were ostensibly
totally excluded from stakeholder participation. Input was not allowed until the decisions
had been made. And yet it is the intervenor witnessing that is not to be trusted?


       6. “It fails to even acknowledge ERCOT’s subsequent recommendations in the 2024
          and 2025 RTP, where ERCOT continues to recommend the three 765 kV import
          paths as projects that are needed by 2030 to maintain transmission reliability
          statewide.13 Finally, the PFD’s need analysis also disregards the legislative
          intent that the PBRP be completed expeditiously, as embodied in PURA §§
          39.166(b) and 37.057.” (page 16).

The applicants’ assertion is partially correct in this regard: ERCOT continues to recommend
all three Import Paths. The wording is strategic and performative. Though the Applicants
may present or imply otherwise, ERCOT does not identify Import Path 2 as a critical or
imminently required part of the PBRP. It instead says it is recommended. “Recommended”
does not denote urgent or critical need. “Recommended” does not even denote required
need. Recommended is anything but a proven need.

       7. “The Import Path 2 Projects were designed as part of an integrated transmission
          solution. The PBRP is an integrated reliability plan. (Emphases added) A
          standalone partial-build study isolating the Import Path 2 Projects would test a
                                          [5]
               different system from the one ERCOT and the Commission evaluated and is not
              required by PURA or the Commission’s rules.” (page 32).

   The common thread assertion of an integrated reliability plan arises again. Green, earlier
   in Docket 59029, did not disagree with the notion the PBRP was a single integrated plan
   with interdependent Import Paths and CCN Dockets. Green’s Motion to Intervene and the
   ALJ’s granting of that Motion in Docket 59029 used the same assertion. Green’s once
   upon a time agreement with the notion, however, is irrelevant. Green argued this exact
   position repeatedly in Docket 59029. As demonstrated below, based on an appeal by
   Oncor to the PUC, the PUC has already ruled otherwise.

C. Findings of Facts:

 The summary: Green concurred, at one point, that the PBRP was integrated and the Import
 Paths were interdependent. Green’s arguments, and those concurring opinions of the presiding
 ALJs in two Dockets (59029 and 59182), were, upon appeal by Oncor to the PUC, overruled
 by the PUC itself.

 1. Chronology, Docket 59029:

        a. Intervenor Tom Green timely filed a motion to intervene on January 12, 2026 (Item
           100).

        b. Oncor (sole Applicant) filed a clarification request on January 14, 2026 (Item 110).

        c. Green timely filed an amended motion to intervene on January 22, 2026 (Item 136).
           Relevant excerpts are below.

               “Oncor argues that landowners outside the immediate one hundred sixty mile
               Longshore-Drill Hole segment lack standing. However, this part of the project
               is but a constituent part of the overall Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP)
               (emphasis added). The PUC has approved the PBRP as a single, integrated
               765 kV loop (emphasis added), an approval affirmed by PUC Executive
               Director Connie Corona on November 12, 2025, stating in part, “. . . the Bell
               County East project cited in your letter is part of a reliability plan . . .”
               (underscore added). Oncor’s segmentation strategy to file separate CCN
               applications does not sever the "real and substantial controversy" regarding
               the loop's cumulative impact on Movant Tom Green’s property interests in
               Schleicher and Burnet Counties, Texas, property for which Movant was noticed
               by Oncor and others as being affected by one of the proposed routes. The
               engineering standards, environmental integrity, and "need" established in this
               proceeding may become a binding precedent for other routes, including the Bell
               County East to Big Hill segment, which directly affects Movant’s property
               interests and is scheduled for CCN filing in March 2026. It is therefore
               reasonable that Movant be allowed to participate now, as now is the time when
               additional evidence can be presented which can affect possible improvements
               to the PBRP.

                                            [6]
       “If Movant is excluded from this proceeding, the "need" and technical
      framework for the 765 kV loop will potentially be finalized before Movant has
      an opportunity to be heard in later proceedings addressing the Bell County East
      to Big Hill segment of the PBRP. Because these segments are electrically,
      physically, and logically interdependent (emphasis added), the ultimate
      outcome of this proceeding may be argued to have a determinate, or domino
      effect, upon the routing and engineering requirements of later segments,
      including the Bell County East to Big Hill segment.” (Pages 4 and 5)

d. SOAH granted Green’s motion to intervene on February 6, 2026 (Item 257, SOAH
   Order No. 12). Relevant excerpts are below.

         “For the reasons discussed below, the motions to intervene of ASL, ABB
         Ranches, and Mr. Green are GRANTED…” (Page 2)
         “Yet, a direct effect on a landowner’s property is not required. (Page 3) 6”

         “ABB Ranches and Mr. Green own land that may be directly impacted by one or
         more routes along proposed transmission lines that are part of the PBRP, but they do
         not own land along the route of the Project at issue in this case.12 Mr. Green
         contends that, because the PBRP is segmented into separate CCN cases, the
         determinations regarding issues such as engineering standards,
         environmental integrity, and need established in this case may become binding
         precedent (emphasis added) for other PBRP routes, including the route that
         directly affects his property interests. ABB Ranches similarly maintains that the
         potential approval of the Project will impact “downstream” landowners (i.e.,
         those who own land along proposed transmission lines that will connect to the
         Project). (Page 6)


         “In response, Oncor asserts that, even if approval of the Project would
         somehow determine, or at least influence, the outcome of future proceedings,
         it would not give ABB Ranches or Mr. Green a justiciable interest in this
         proceeding because the Project will not cross over or near their properties and,
         therefore, cannot deprive them of their property or directly cause them any actual
         or probable harm. (Page 6)


         “The ALJ concludes that ABB Ranches and Mr. Green demonstrated a
         justiciable interest. (Emphasis added.) (“Demonstrated” here is based on the
         PBRP being a single integrated and interdependent Plan. Parenthetical added
         for summary.) One factor the Commission must consider in this case is “the
         need for additional service…” (Page 6)13

         “Notably, the Commission has previously granted a contested motion to intervene
         where, despite the intervening party not having a direct interest in the outcome of
         the proceeding, it showed that the case would set policy that would implicate future
         cases addressing the same issue that the intervening party would be subject to.14

                                     [7]
                  The ALJ finds the current situation to be analogous. Intervention in this
                 circumstance is also consistent with liberally construing a party’s right to appear
                 in agency proceedings. (Pages 6, 7)15”

       e. Oncor appealed the SOAH’s granting of Green’s motion on February 17, 2026
          (Item 276, SOAH Order NO. 12). Notably, this appeal was directly to the PUC.

       f. Green timely responded to Oncor’s appeal on February 24, 2026 (Item 319).

       g. The Hearing on the Merits occurred on March 2 through 4, 2026. Notably, the
          Hearing in which Green fully participated was completed before Green was, a week
          later, denied by the PUC the justiciable interest granted him by the SOAH.

       h. On March 3, 2026 (Item 373), the PUC gave notice that it would consider the merits
          of Oncor’s appeal in the PUC’s Open Meeting scheduled for March 12, 2026.

       i. On March 9, 2026, Green timely requested 5 minutes of oral argument for the
          March 12, 2026 Open Meeting (Item 387). Green’s request specifically relied upon
          the appeal being “set on the agenda.”

       j. On March 10, 2026 (Item 404), one day after Green’s request for oral arguments,
          the PUC noticed it would not hear oral arguments on Oncor’s appeal of SOAH
          Order No. 12. Another intervenor ASL, American Stewards of Liberty, likewise
          requested oral argument. Not so parenthetically, the question could be asked why
          only the intervenors made a timely request for oral argument? Why did applicant
          Oncor not also make such request? Might it have been that Oncor already knew, by
          ex-parte communication or by Commission history on such matters, that the PUC’s
          decision would favor its appeal. Regardless of the answer to that question, the PUC
          did side with the Oncor appeal in the Open Meeting of March 12, 2926, thereby
          overruling the decisions of at least three ALJs (One in Docket 59029 and two in
          Docket 59182).

       k. The written order overruling the SOAH was filed on April 8, 2026 (Item 426). The
          relevant excerpt is below.


                 “Therefore, the Commission partially grants Oncor's appeal of SOAH Order
                 No. 12 to reverse the ALJ's decision (emphasis added) to grant the
                 intervention of Mr. Green. The Commission denies Tom Green's motion to
                 intervene.(Emphasis added)”(Page 3)

D. Importance of the Docket 59029 to Import Path 2 Dockets 59182 and 59475.

    Why is this evidentiary record regarding the interdependence of the three Import Paths of
    importance? The answer is because the PUC has already ruled, implicitly in its denial of
    Green’s Motion to Intervene in Docker 59029, that the Import Paths are not
    interdependent. To wit.

      a. Green’s amended motion to intervene was granted by three ALJs, (first) in Docket
                                        [8]
            59029 and subsequently in Docket 59182. Briefly, Green’s premise for his motion
           to intervene and the SOAH’s subsequent granting was that the Permian Basin
           Reliability Plan (PBRP) was approved by the PUC as a single integrated plan, and,
           accordingly, all three Import Paths were interdependent. Therefore, any of the 5
           PBRP Dockets could affect findings in subsequent Dockets. Said differently, a
           decision for a CCN covering a remote and less populated area of the State could
           affect Green’s rights on a route in another part of the State. It was the “domino”
           potential. The three ALJs agreed.

       b. The integrated interdependence argument initially presented by Green, which was
          subsequently denied based on the Oncor appeal directly to the PUC, is now the same
          argument the Applicants attempt to apply to the current Docket. Notably, Oncor is
          an Applicant in 59029.

       c. The PUC, in its March 12, 2026 Open Meeting, ruled, without allowing oral
          arguments for discovery, Green’s position and the ALJs’ concurrence were both in
          error. The undeniable and inescapable result of that decision is that the PBRP is not
          an integrated and interdependent plan requiring all three Import Paths. The
          decision is definitive precedence that Docket 59029 could not affect subsequent
          Dockets, and contra-positively, other Dockets could not affect 59029. The same
          holds for Import Paths.

       d. Green was denied his justiciable interests expressly and decidedly because the PUC
          ruled that the three Import Paths are not integrated and interdependent, that one could
          not be used to implicate another. The Import Paths are, according to the PUC’s own
          ruling, independent.

E. Conclusions of Law

 HB 5066 required ERCOT to develop a Permian Basin reliability plan and required the PUCT
 to develop a plan for implementing adopted reliability plans. It did not select 765 kV, approve
 Import Path 2, order construction of every project ERCOT recommended, or eliminate the
 applicants’ burden of proof obligation to obtain a project-specific CCN under PURA §37.056.

 A “Plan to implement” is not “approval of every CCN.”

 The Commission’s approval of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and its subsequent approval
 of CCNs for the projects comprising Import Path 1 do not, as a matter of law, establish that the
 Import Path 2 projects satisfy the necessity requirements of PURA §37.056. Each application
 requires a determination, based on the evidentiary record in that proceeding, that the requested
 certificate is proven necessary. The PBRP and the Commission’s orders concerning Import
 Path 1 in no way relieve Applicants of their burden to establish the critical and urgent need for
 Import Path 2 in these proceedings. The evidentiary records do not satisfy that burden of proof.

 The PBRP does not somehow negate the CCN process and automatically prove need.



                                             [9]
  The Commission’s Orders on Appeal in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59182 recognize common
 CCN considerations between the two end-to-end component projects comprising each
 individual import path. Those orders do not establish that approval of one import path in any
 way conclusively determines the statutory necessity of a different import path.

 The Legislature prescribed the process and policy direction; it did not predetermine a particular
 certificate.

 Applicants’ contention that denying Import Path 2 would “undermine” an integrated plan is not
 only counter to the PUC’s denial of Green’s Motion to Intervene in Docket 59029, but it
 furthermore does not answer the statutory question. System planning or interaction may make
 the PBRP probative, but it does not make the PBRP conclusive. If prior approval of the
 PBRP had already adjudicated the necessity of every included project, the Legislature’s
 requirement that Applicants obtain individual CCNs under PURA §37.056… and the
 Commission’s referral of need issues for contested-case adjudication… would serve no
 meaningful purpose.

 The Applicants are effectively attempting to elevate the PBRP from one element in the
 evidentiary record into a prior universal binding determination that covers all Import Paths.
 Such an elevation does not satisfy PURA §37.056. A proven need is still required for the
 certificate sought in Docket 59475. That independent need has not been proven.

F. Prayer

 Green’s Prayer is simple. It is straightforward. The evidentiary record and Conclusions of Law,
 as demonstrated above, illustrate Green’s Prayer is already decided.

 The SOAH got it right in its PFD.

 In “plain language,” as cited for use many times by the Applicants in their Exceptions, Green
 respectfully implores the SOAH to reject all the Applicants’ Proposed Replacement Findings
 in any way based on Import Path 2 being part of an integrated Plan, or in any way materially
 relying on conditions or evidence in other Dockets.

 And given virtually all of the Applicants’ Proposed Exceptions rely on the fundamentally erred
 premise of integrated and interdependent Import Paths, it is asked that all of the Applicants’
 Proposed Exceptions be denied.

 One cannot deny a judiciable interest because the Dockets and Import paths are ruled not
 interdependent, and turn around to subsequently grant a Proposed Exception because the
 Dockets and Import Paths are suddenly interdependent. Doing so would not be right by any
 measure of common law or common decency.

 With utmost respect and high confidence that the SOAH serving the still great State of Texas
 will “do the right thing.”



                                            [10]
     Tom Green
